summary: Defines a static dictionary for Signaling Compression (SigComp) tuned to SIP presence documents. A shared dictionary lets compressors shrink the text-based messages more. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If both people already own the same dictionary of common words, messages can be written much shorter. This is such a dictionary for presence messages.

questions: how to compress sip presence messages
what is the sigcomp presence dictionary
how does a static dictionary help sigcomp
why is the presence dictionary never updated
how much does the presence dictionary improve compression
subtitle: A fixed dictionary of common presence-document strings that gives SigComp a head start on its very first message.

tldr.problem: SigComp compresses SIP messages poorly at first because there is no stored state to compress against, and the existing SIP/SDP dictionary does nothing for the XML presence documents that SIP carries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines one fixed dictionary of well-known presence strings, given in a normative binary form that SigComp loads as a state item, so even the first message can be compressed against it.
tldr.outcome: The author's initial simulations showed about a further 10% compression once SigComp and partial notification or publication were already in use. The dictionary is frozen and never updated.

today: RFC 5112 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text says the dictionary is defined once and stays as it is forever.

sections.title: Why Presence Needs Its Own Dictionary
sections.content:
SIP presence information travels in XML documents, for example the Presence Information Data Format (PIDF) and its many extensions. These documents can be large, depending on how many presentities a watcher follows and how much each one publishes. That hurts on scarce links such as low-bandwidth, high-latency wireless networks.

SigComp (RFC 3320) compresses text protocols such as SIP, but its compression only reaches its best rate after a few message exchanges, because the first message has no stored state to compress against. RFC 3485 already provides a static dictionary for SIP and SDP, but it has no effect on XML presence documents. This RFC fills that gap.
sections.eli5: Presence messages are long, and the first one is hard to squeeze because the other side has not seen anything yet. A shared word list fixes that.

sections.title: Design of the Dictionary
sections.content:
The presence-specific static dictionary is a collection of well-known strings that appear in most SIP presence documents. It is not a complete list of reserved words. It MAY be available in SigComp implementations that support presence, and it can coexist with the SIP/SDP dictionary of RFC 3485. SigComp endpoints announce one or both dictionaries until the other end acknowledges the announcement.

The dictionary is not meant to evolve. It is defined once and stays as it is forever, which avoids the problem of finding out which of several versions the remote end supports.

Several choices shape the string list:

  • Only strings of four or more characters are used, because most compression algorithms break even at around three or four characters.
  • The < and > signs of XML elements are left out, so one string serves start-tags, start-tags with attributes, empty-element tags and end-tags.
  • Enumerated values are stored without their quotes.
  • Some strings, such as IETF URNs, are split so that parts can be reused.
sections.eli5: The list is made once and never changed, so both sides always know exactly what is in it. It only holds longer words, because tiny words are not worth looking up.

sections.title: Input Strings and Priorities
sections.content:
Appendix A is informative. It lists every input string as a UTF-8 string with a priority (Pr), a hexadecimal offset (Off), a length in octets (Len) and references to the specifications that define the string. Strings are case sensitive. Many come from PIDF and its extensions, such as presence, tuple, status and basic, plus the mood, activity and place names of rich presence.

Priorities run from 1 to 5. A low value means the string is very likely to appear in a presence document. A high value marks less frequent extensions or optional XML elements and attributes. The priorities exist because some algorithms, such as DEFLATE, work better when the most common strings sit at the bottom of the dictionary. Strings with a suitable common substring can share space, so offsets overlap.
sections.eli5: Each word gets a score from 1 to 5 for how often it is likely to show up. The common ones go in a handy spot at the end of the list.

sections.title: The Binary Dictionary State
sections.content:
Section 4 gives the normative binary form, loaded into SigComp as a state. It has two parts, concatenated to form the state value: a string subset holding all the strings as substrings (roughly ordered so that low-priority-number strings come at the end), and a table subset of length and offset pairs. Each length is one byte. Each offset is two bytes with 1024 added, so values can be used directly if the state is loaded at address 1024.

All compression algorithms can use the string subset. Methods in the LZ78 family can also use the table to form an initial set of tokens. The state item has state_identifier 0xd942297d0bb38fc01d6741d6b3b48157ac8e1be0, state_length 0x0D93 and minimum_access_length 6. The string subset is 0x0955 bytes and the table subset is 0x043E bytes.

Both parts are read with a STATE-ACCESS instruction, where the memory pointed to by %ps holds 0xd942297d0bb3. A compressor that wants less UDVM memory can take only the strings up to a chosen priority by changing the offset and length operands, using values given in a priority table.
sections.eli5: The list is stored as one block of bytes: the words first, then a table saying where each word starts and how long it is. You can also copy only the most important words if you are short on space.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC only defines a static dictionary for the SigComp framework, so the security considerations of RFC 3320 apply. The memo states that it does not introduce any known additional security risk.
sections.eli5: The word list adds no new dangers. The same safety rules as for SigComp itself apply.
